phil.epistemology.bayesian.the-bet-you-c.title: The bet you are guaranteed to lose
phil.epistemology.bayesian.the-bet-you-c.hook: If your degrees of belief break the probability axioms, a stranger can sell you bets you each call fair and still take your money.
phil.epistemology.bayesian.the-bet-you-c.author: author-humanities-1

reviewed.notes: Opened on a definition; reordered so the Dutch book exploit leads and the credence framing follows.

phil.epistemology.bayesian.the-bet-you-c.body:
Suppose you would take a fair bet at 0.6 that it rains tomorrow, and also a fair bet at 0.6 that it does not. Both feel reasonable in isolation. Sell me both and I pay you two stakes worth 1.2, collect one back whatever happens, and you have lost 0.2 with certainty. No forecast was needed. Only your arithmetic was wrong.

The trick works because Bayesian epistemology measures belief in exactly that currency: belief is not on or off, it comes in degrees, and your degree of belief in a claim is revealed by the odds at which you would bet on it either way. Once that is the unit, being incoherent stops being a vague failing and becomes a hole in your wallet.

That is a **Dutch book**, and Frank Ramsey in 1926 and Bruno de Finetti in 1937 showed the general result: you are immune to it exactly when your degrees of belief satisfy the probability axioms. Rationality, on this view, is not about being right. It is about not being exploitable.

Then the second question: what should belief do when evidence arrives?
phil.epistemology.bayesian.the-bet-you-c.rigor:
Let $\mathrm{Cr}$ be your credence function over an algebra of propositions, and treat $\mathrm{Cr}(A)$ as the price you consider fair for a ticket paying $1$ if $A$ and $0$ otherwise.

**Synchronic Dutch book theorem (Ramsey, de Finetti).** There exists a finite set of bets, each acceptable at your prices, with a guaranteed net loss, if and only if $\mathrm{Cr}$ violates non-negativity, normalisation, or finite additivity. The rain example is the additivity failure with $A$ and $\neg A$.

**Conditionalisation.** On learning $E$ and nothing stronger, set
$$\mathrm{Cr}_{\text{new}}(H) \;=\; \mathrm{Cr}(H \mid E) \;=\; \frac{\mathrm{Cr}(E \mid H)\,\mathrm{Cr}(H)}{\mathrm{Cr}(E)}.$$
David Lewis's diachronic Dutch book argument, published by Teller in 1973, extends the exploitation result: announce in advance any updating rule other than conditionalisation and a bookmaker can construct a package of bets, some placed before the evidence and some after, that loses you money for sure.

The honest limits are two. Where the prior $\mathrm{Cr}(H)$ comes from is unanswered — coherence constrains it barely at all. And convergence theorems saying disagreeing agents are eventually driven together by data assume everyone gives the truth a non-zero prior, which is precisely what a dogmatist refuses.

recall.question: What does a Dutch book argument actually establish about incoherent credences?

options.text: That they will make you wrong more often
options.why: incoherence is a structural defect, not a track record.

options.text: That a set of bets exists which you call fair one by one and which loses you money whatever happens
options.why: no prediction required.

options.text: That they violate the laws of logic
options.why: probability axioms are stronger than consistency; you can be logically consistent and still incoherent.

phil.epistemology.bayesian.the-test-that.title: The test came back positive. Now what?
phil.epistemology.bayesian.the-test-that.hook: A test that is right 90% of the time just came back positive. Your turn: how worried should you be?
phil.epistemology.bayesian.the-test-that.author: author-humanities-1

reviewed.notes: Recall asked for a count and the reveal answered with a share; question aligned.

phil.epistemology.bayesian.the-test-that.body:
A condition affects 1 in 100 people. There is a screening test. If you have the condition, it flags you 90% of the time. If you do not, it still flags you 9% of the time.

You get screened, with no symptoms and no reason to suspect anything. The test is positive.

Before reading on, write down a number: what is the probability that you actually have the condition? Most people, including a famous share of doctors asked this in studies, answer somewhere between 70% and 90%.

Do not reach for the formula. Imagine 1,000 people walking through the door and just count them.

recall.question: Out of 1,000 screened people, what share of the positives are real?
recall.answer: About 9%. Of 1,000 people, 10 have the condition and 9 of them test positive. Of the 990 healthy ones, 9% — about 89 people — also test positive. So roughly 98 positives, of which 9 are real: 9 in 98, near 9%. The test is accurate; the base rate is tiny, and the tiny base rate wins.

phil.epistemology.gettier.three-pages-in.title: Three pages in 1963, and the definition collapsed
phil.epistemology.gettier.three-pages-in.hook: Three pages, two examples, and a definition that had stood since Plato stopped working.
phil.epistemology.gettier.three-pages-in.author: author-humanities-1
phil.epistemology.gettier.three-pages-in.body:
Knowledge is justified true belief. Believe it, be right, and have good reason — that was the working definition for a very long time. In 1963 Edmund Gettier, a young lecturer who had published nothing, sent three pages to the journal *Analysis*. Two counterexamples, no theory, no fix offered.

Here is the first. Smith has excellent evidence that Jones will get the job, and has counted ten coins in Jones's pocket. So he believes, with good reason, that the man who will get the job has ten coins in his pocket. In fact Smith gets the job — and, unknown to him, Smith has ten coins in his own pocket.

His belief is true. It is justified. And calling it knowledge feels absurd, because it came out true by accident, through a route that had nothing to do with why he believed it.

What Gettier exposed is that ordinary justification does not exclude luck. Sixty years of repairs have followed — no false premises, reliable processes, safety, sensitivity, defeasibility — and Linda Zagzebski argued in 1994 that any account combining truth with fallible justification will regenerate the problem.

recall.question: What exactly does a Gettier case show?

options.text: That justified beliefs are often false
options.why: Gettier's beliefs are all true; that is the point.

options.text: That a belief can be true, justified, and true only by luck
options.why: so justification plus truth does not add up to knowledge.

options.text: That knowledge requires certainty
options.why: Gettier does not demand infallibility; he shows fallible justification lets luck in.

phil.epistemology.induction.every-emeral.title: Every emerald you have ever seen is also grue
phil.epistemology.induction.every-emeral.hook: Every emerald ever examined is green. Every emerald ever examined is also grue. Pick one, and you have predicted different futures.
phil.epistemology.induction.every-emeral.author: author-humanities-1

reviewed.notes: The rigor quantified over an undefined predicate Ex'; renotated with Mx for 'is an emerald'.

phil.epistemology.induction.every-emeral.body:
Hume asked whether past regularities license future predictions. Nelson Goodman asked a nastier question in 1955: *which* regularity did you even observe?

Define **grue**: an object is grue if it has been examined before some future time $t$ and is green, or has not been examined before $t$ and is blue. Now look at your evidence. Every emerald ever examined has been green. Every emerald ever examined has also, by that definition, been grue. The evidence is identical, letter for letter.

But "all emeralds are green" predicts that the next emerald, examined after $t$, will be green, and "all emeralds are grue" predicts it will be blue. Same data, opposite forecasts, equal support.

The instinct is to say grue is artificial — defined with a clock in it. That instinct does not survive contact. Someone whose primitive vocabulary is *grue* and *bleen* can define green as "examined before $t$ and grue, or not so examined and bleen". Which pair is the gerrymandered one depends on where you start.
phil.epistemology.induction.every-emeral.rigor:
Formally, let $Mx$ be "x is an emerald", $Gx$ "x is green", $Bx$ "x is blue" and $Ex$ "x is examined before $t$". Define
$$G^{*}x \;\equiv\; (Ex \wedge Gx) \vee (\neg Ex \wedge Bx).$$
For every observed emerald $a$ we have $Ea$, so $Ga \leftrightarrow G^{*}a$. Any confirmation relation that depends only on the observed instances therefore confirms $\forall x (Mx \to Gx)$ and $\forall x (Mx \to G^{*}x)$ to exactly the same degree — yet they diverge on every unexamined case.

Goodman's conclusion is that confirmation is not a purely syntactic relation between evidence and hypothesis. Some predicates are **projectible** and some are not, and no amount of logic separates them, because the symmetry above shows the "positional" defect is relative to the chosen primitives.

His own answer is **entrenchment**: a predicate is projectible to the extent that it and its relatives have actually been used in successful past projections. That is frankly a historical fact about our language, not a logical one — which is either the honest answer or a surrender, depending on who you ask. Bayesians reply that priors do the work; the grue problem then reappears as the question of why your prior over hypotheses looks like that.

recall.question: Why does calling "grue" artificial fail to settle the new riddle?
recall.answer: Because the artificiality is symmetric. Starting from grue and bleen as primitives, green is the one that needs a time-indexed definition. Nothing purely logical marks one vocabulary as the natural one, which is exactly Goodman's point.

phil.epistemology.induction.the-sun-has-.title: The sun has made you no promises
phil.epistemology.induction.the-sun-has-.hook: Ask why the sun will rise tomorrow and every answer you give quietly assumes the thing it is supposed to prove.
phil.epistemology.induction.the-sun-has-.author: author-humanities-1
phil.epistemology.induction.the-sun-has-.body:
Why will the sun rise tomorrow? Because it always has. Fine — but that argument needs a bridge: the future resembles the past. Where did you get that? From the fact that, so far, the future has resembled the past. You have just used induction to justify induction.

David Hume laid this out in the *Treatise* of 1739 and again, more readably, in the *Enquiry* of 1748, and nobody has got around it since. Deduction cannot help: it is not contradictory to suppose the sun fails to rise. Experience cannot help either, because every appeal to experience already presupposes the uniformity in question.

Hume's own conclusion is stranger than scepticism. He does not tell you to stop expecting sunrise; he says the expectation was never the work of reason. It is custom — a habit of mind produced by repetition, the same mechanism a dog has. Reason discovers the gap and then watches you step over it anyway.

You might think the damage is confined to whether the future resembles the past. In 1955 Nelson Goodman showed it is worse: even *past* evidence does not tell you which regularity you have observed.

recall.question: Why can't "nature has been uniform so far" justify expecting nature to stay uniform?

options.text: Because using past uniformity to predict future uniformity is the very inference under question
options.why: the argument is circular.

options.text: Because nature is not in fact uniform
options.why: Hume's problem stands even in a perfectly uniform world.

options.text: Because the past evidence is incomplete
options.why: completeness would not help; no finite record entails anything about the next case.

phil.ethics.trolley-dilemmas.nobody-in-1.title: Nobody in 1967 was asking about a lever
phil.ethics.trolley-dilemmas.nobody-in-1.hook: In Foot's original case you are the driver, not a bystander, and the paper is not about trolleys at all.
phil.ethics.trolley-dilemmas.nobody-in-1.author: author-humanities-1
phil.ethics.trolley-dilemmas.nobody-in-1.body:
Philippa Foot's 1967 paper is called "The Problem of Abortion and the Doctrine of the Double Effect", it appeared in the *Oxford Review*, and the runaway tram is one example among several. Her case is not the one you know: you are the **driver** of a tram whose brakes have failed, and you can steer onto one of two tracks, five workers on one and one on the other. What interested her was the old distinction between harm you intend and harm you merely foresee.

Judith Jarvis Thomson moved the reader out of the cab. In "Killing, Letting Die, and the Trolley Problem" (*The Monist*, 1976) and "The Trolley Problem" (*Yale Law Journal*, 1985), the agent becomes a bystander at a switch, and she added the footbridge: a large man whose body would stop the trolley. Same arithmetic, five for one, and almost everyone's intuition flips.

Then the part that never gets told. In "Turning the Trolley" (2008) Thomson changed her mind and argued the bystander may *not* turn it. The case's own inventor stopped accepting the standard answer.

recall.question: How does Foot's original trolley case differ from the one everyone cites?
recall.answer: In Foot (1967) the agent is the tram's driver, already steering a lethal vehicle, and the example serves a paper on abortion and the doctrine of double effect. Thomson (1976, 1985) introduced the bystander at the switch and the footbridge variant — and in 2008 argued the bystander should not turn it.

sources.title: The Problem of Abortion and the Doctrine of the Double Effect
sources.author: Philippa Foot

phil.history.presocratics.thales-and-the.title: If you are so clever, why aren't you rich?
phil.history.presocratics.thales-and-the.hook: The first philosopher answered the question 'if you are so clever, why aren't you rich?' by cornering a market.
phil.history.presocratics.thales-and-the.author: author-humanities-1
phil.history.presocratics.thales-and-the.body:
Aristotle tells this in the *Politics*, Book I, and tells it precisely because people mocked philosophy as useless. Thales of Miletus, the story goes, read the signs and judged that the coming olive harvest would be enormous. In the dead of winter, when nobody wanted them, he put deposits on every olive press in Miletus and Chios, cheaply, because there was no competition for them.

The harvest came in huge. Everyone needed a press at once, and Thales rented them out on his own terms.

Aristotle's moral is double-edged. Philosophers could easily get rich if they thought it worth bothering with — and, he adds, what Thales really demonstrated is a general recipe that has nothing to do with wisdom: create a monopoly.

Treat it as an anecdote, not a record; Aristotle is writing two and a half centuries later. But look at the structure. Thales paid a small sum for the right, not the obligation, to use a press later at a fixed price. That is a call option, priced by a man who had no word for it.

recall.question: What financial instrument does the Thales story describe?
recall.answer: A call option. He paid a small premium in winter for the right to use the presses at an agreed price at harvest, with no obligation if the crop failed. Aristotle reports it as proof that philosophers could get rich, and notes the real lesson is monopoly.

phil.logic.paradoxes.the-sentence-that-c.title: The sentence that cannot be either
phil.logic.paradoxes.the-sentence-that-c.hook: Nine words that no consistent theory of truth can survive: this sentence is not true.
phil.logic.paradoxes.the-sentence-that-c.author: author-humanities-1

reviewed.notes: Difficulty 2 to 3: the rigor is the diagonal lemma plus Tarski undefinability with Godel numbering.

phil.logic.paradoxes.the-sentence-that-c.body:
*This sentence is not true.*

If it is true, then what it says holds, so it is not true. If it is not true, then what it says holds, so it is true. Eubulides of Miletus was playing with this in the fourth century BCE, and for two thousand years it looked like a parlour trick.

It is not a trick. Take three assumptions that every ordinary account of truth makes: sentences can refer to themselves, every sentence is either true or not, and "S is true" holds exactly when S. The liar shows these three cannot all stand together. So the damage is not to one odd sentence; it is to the concept of truth as a predicate of a language that can talk about itself.

The repairs are all painful. Ban self-reference, and you lose harmless and useful sentences. Ban the middle, and you must explain what the liar is instead. Keep everything and accept that some sentences are both true and false — which is what dialetheists like Graham Priest actually propose.

Here is the sharpest version, where the paradox becomes a theorem.
phil.logic.paradoxes.the-sentence-that-c.rigor:
Fix a theory $T$ in a language $L$, strong enough to represent its own syntax (arithmetic suffices, via Gödel numbering, with $\ulcorner S \urcorner$ the code of $S$).

**Diagonal lemma.** For any formula $\varphi(x)$ of $L$ with one free variable, there is a sentence $S$ with
$$T \vdash S \leftrightarrow \varphi(\ulcorner S \urcorner).$$

**Tarski's undefinability theorem (1933).** There is no formula $\mathrm{True}(x)$ of $L$ such that $T \vdash \mathrm{True}(\ulcorner S\urcorner) \leftrightarrow S$ for every sentence $S$, unless $T$ is inconsistent.

*Proof sketch.* Suppose such a $\mathrm{True}$ exists. Apply the diagonal lemma to $\neg\mathrm{True}(x)$ to get $L^{*}$ with $T \vdash L^{*} \leftrightarrow \neg \mathrm{True}(\ulcorner L^{*}\urcorner)$. Combine with the truth schema for $L^{*}$ and you derive $L^{*} \leftrightarrow \neg L^{*}$.

That is the liar, promoted from a puzzle to a proof: truth for $L$ is not definable inside $L$. Tarski's own response is a hierarchy — define truth for $L$ in a stronger metalanguage, then truth for that in a stronger one still. Saul Kripke's 1975 alternative builds truth as a least fixed point of a monotone operator, leaving the liar simply ungrounded: it never receives a value at any stage. Neither is free. The hierarchy cannot express "everything Jones says is false"; the fixed point cannot express "the liar is ungrounded" without a new liar appearing one level up.

recall.question: What does Tarski's undefinability theorem show about the liar?

options.text: That self-referential sentences are meaningless
options.why: Tarski proves a limit on definability, not a theory of meaning.

options.text: That a sufficiently strong consistent language cannot contain its own truth predicate
options.why: so the liar is a theorem about expressive limits.

options.text: That arithmetic is inconsistent
options.why: the theorem is conditional on consistency and gives no reason to doubt it.

sources.title: Outline of a Theory of Truth
sources.author: Saul Kripke

phil.mind.chinese-room.the-man-who-memor.title: The man who memorised the whole rulebook
phil.mind.chinese-room.the-man-who-memor.hook: Searle's reply to his critics was to swallow the room: memorise every rule, work outdoors, still understand nothing.
phil.mind.chinese-room.the-man-who-memor.author: author-humanities-1
phil.mind.chinese-room.the-man-who-memor.body:
John Searle, 1980, in *Behavioral and Brain Sciences*. You are locked in a room. Chinese characters come in under the door. An enormous English rulebook tells you which characters to send back out. You follow it perfectly, and outside, fluent Chinese speakers conclude they are having a conversation.

You do not understand a word of Chinese. And, says Searle, neither does any computer running any program, however good the conversation, because a program is exactly that rulebook: syntax all the way down, with no meaning attached anywhere.

The strongest objection is the **systems reply**: of course *you* do not understand Chinese, any more than a neuron understands English. The understanding, if any, belongs to the whole system — person plus rulebook plus paper.

Searle's counter is to eliminate the system. Memorise the rulebook. Do the lookups in your head. Walk out of the room. Now you *are* the entire system, and you still do not understand a word.

Whether that works is one of the longest arguments in the field. Many think it assumes the conclusion: that if understanding were there, whoever runs the computation would notice.

recall.question: What is Searle's response to the systems reply?

options.text: That the room is too slow to count as understanding
options.why: Searle explicitly says speed is irrelevant to the argument.

options.text: Internalise the whole system
options.why: memorise the rules and do it all in your head, and the man simply is the system, still without understanding.

options.text: That no rulebook could ever pass as fluent
options.why: the thought experiment grants that it does; that is what makes it interesting.

phil.mind.functionalism-computation.gode.title: Remember Gödel's sentence? It does not prove you are not a machine
phil.mind.functionalism-computation.gode.hook: Remember Gödel's unprovable sentence? Two well-known arguments use it to prove you are not a machine, and both leak in the same place.
phil.mind.functionalism-computation.gode.author: author-humanities-1

reviewed.notes: Difficulty 2 to 3: the rigor turns on Con(F) and the second incompleteness theorem.

phil.mind.functionalism-computation.gode.body:
When you met incompleteness, the headline was that any consistent formal system strong enough for arithmetic contains a true sentence it cannot prove. J. R. Lucas in 1961, and Roger Penrose in two books in 1989 and 1994, turned that into an argument about minds.

It goes: suppose your mind is some formal system $F$. Then there is a sentence $G(F)$ that $F$ cannot prove. But you, looking at $F$, can see that $G(F)$ is true. So you can do something $F$ cannot, so you are not $F$. And since $F$ was arbitrary, you are not any machine.

The leak is in "can see that it is true". Gödel's theorem does not hand you a true sentence for free; it hands you a conditional. And the condition is exactly the thing you are not in a position to check about a machine as complicated as a brain.
phil.mind.functionalism-computation.gode.rigor:
Let $F$ be a recursively axiomatised, consistent theory extending Robinson arithmetic. The first incompleteness theorem produces a sentence $G(F)$ with
$$F \nvdash G(F) \quad \text{and} \quad F \nvdash \neg G(F),$$
and what is actually provable in a weak metatheory is the conditional
$$\mathrm{Con}(F) \;\to\; G(F).$$

So to "see that $G(F)$ is true" you must first know $\mathrm{Con}(F)$. Three consequences sink the argument.

First, by the second incompleteness theorem $F$ cannot prove $\mathrm{Con}(F)$ — but neither can you, for an $F$ the size of a candidate brain-program presented as a huge axiom list. Nothing in the situation gives you the required insight.

Second, the mechanist's claim is only that *some* $F$ matches your output, not that you can identify it. Hilary Putnam's response in 1960 already made this point: you would have to know your own program, and know it to be consistent.

Third, human mathematicians are demonstrably inconsistent — they publish false proofs — and inconsistency makes $G(F)$ derivable along with everything else, so the argument's premise fails at the start.

None of this proves functionalism is right. It shows that incompleteness, which is a theorem about provability inside fixed formal systems, is not a theorem about what minds can see.

recall.question: Where does the Lucas-Penrose argument break down?

options.text: Gödel's theorem applies only to arithmetic, not to brains
options.why: it applies to any system interpreting enough arithmetic, so that is not the objection.

options.text: Seeing that the Gödel sentence is true requires knowing the system is consistent
options.why: and nobody can establish that for a brain-sized formal system, including themselves.

options.text: The Gödel sentence is not really true
options.why: it is true in the standard model, given consistency; the dispute is about who can know that.

phil.political.latin-american-thought.ar.title: Ariel, Calibán y quién decide el símbolo
phil.political.latin-american-thought.ar.hook: Rodó le dio a América Latina un símbolo en 1900. Setenta años después, Fernández Retamar le devolvió el que el maestro había descartado.
phil.political.latin-american-thought.ar.author: author-humanities-1

reviewed.notes: 1898 corrected: the US did not keep Cuba. Puerto Rico and the Philippines were ceded; Cuba was under military occupation. Trimmed back inside the word limit.

phil.political.latin-american-thought.ar.body:
En 1900, dos años después de que Estados Unidos ganara la guerra contra España, se quedara con Puerto Rico y Filipinas y dejara a Cuba bajo ocupación, el uruguayo José Enrique Rodó publicó *Ariel*. Un maestro, Próspero, se despide de sus discípulos bajo una estatua de Ariel, el espíritu alado de *La tempestad* de Shakespeare. Enfrente, Calibán: lo material, lo utilitario.

El mensaje era para la juventud latinoamericana: no imiten. Rodó llamó *nordomanía* a la fascinación con el modelo estadounidense y propuso que la región cultivara lo que él veía como su herencia grecolatina. El libro fundó el «arielismo» y se volvió lectura obligada en medio continente.

También es fácil de criticar: la propuesta es elitista, mira a Europa y no dice casi nada de los indígenas ni de los negros de la América que decía defender.

Por eso el giro de 1971 es tan bueno. Roberto Fernández Retamar publicó *Calibán* y reclamó el otro símbolo: si el colonizador nos llamó Calibán —el esclavo, el deforme, el que solo aprendió la lengua para maldecir—, pues ese somos, y desde ahí se habla. El mismo Shakespeare, el personaje contrario.

recall.question: ¿Qué le reprocha Fernández Retamar al arielismo de Rodó?

options.text: Que defendiera la independencia política de la región
options.why: los dos la daban por sentada.

options.text: Que eligiera como símbolo al espíritu culto y europeo
options.why: dejando afuera a Calibán, es decir al colonizado real, indígena y negro.

options.text: Que admirara el modelo estadounidense
options.why: Rodó hizo justo lo contrario: advirtió contra la nordomanía.

sources.title: Calibán: apuntes sobre la cultura en nuestra América
sources.author: Roberto Fernández Retamar

phil.political.latin-american-thought.el.title: El problema del indio no era el indio
phil.political.latin-american-thought.el.hook: Mariátegui movió la pregunta indígena de la moral y la escuela a un solo lugar: la propiedad de la tierra.
phil.political.latin-american-thought.el.author: author-humanities-1
phil.political.latin-american-thought.el.body:
Lima, 1928. José Carlos Mariátegui publica *7 ensayos de interpretación de la realidad peruana*, dos años después de fundar la revista *Amauta* y dos antes de morir, a los treinta y cinco, con una pierna amputada y escribiendo desde una silla de ruedas.

El primer ensayo hace un movimiento que todavía sirve. La «cuestión indígena» se discutía entonces como un asunto de raza, de moral cristiana, de educación o de administración. Mariátegui responde que todo eso es decorado: el problema es la propiedad de la tierra, el latifundio y el gamonal que manda sobre la provincia sin que la ley pueda nada. Cambie la estructura agraria y las demás explicaciones se quedan sin objeto.

Lo segundo fue igual de incómodo para los suyos: sostuvo que el socialismo en América no podía ser una traducción del manual europeo, y buscó continuidad entre el ayllu andino y el proyecto socialista. La Comintern lo llamó desviacionista.

Para un economista es un caso limpio de lo que hoy se llamaría análisis institucional: la pregunta no es qué creen las personas, sino quién es dueño de qué y con qué poder de coerción.

recall.question: ¿Cuál es la tesis central del primer ensayo de Mariátegui?

options.text: Que el problema indígena se resuelve con educación y alfabetización
options.why: es justamente la explicación que él descarta como insuficiente.

options.text: Que es un problema de tierra
options.why: el latifundio y el gamonalismo, no la raza, la moral ni la escuela.

options.text: Que Perú debía copiar el modelo soviético
options.why: Mariátegui rechazó la copia y por eso chocó con la Comintern.

sources.title: 7 ensayos de interpretación de la realidad peruana
sources.author: José Carlos Mariátegui

phil.political.liberty.two-questions-tha.title: Two questions that sound like one
phil.political.liberty.two-questions-tha.hook: Free from what, and free to do what, are not two halves of one question. Berlin thought the second one had a body count.
phil.political.liberty.two-questions-tha.author: author-humanities-1
phil.political.liberty.two-questions-tha.body:
Isaiah Berlin gave his inaugural lecture at Oxford on 31 October 1958 and separated two things the word *liberty* had been carrying at once.

**Negative liberty** answers: what is the area in which I am left alone? It is measured by absence — no one blocking the door, no law forbidding the book. **Positive liberty** answers a different question: who is master here? It is about self-direction, about being the author of your own life rather than a passenger.

Both sound good. Berlin's warning is about a slide in the second. If freedom is self-mastery, and the self that counts is the rational one, someone can claim to know what you would want if you were thinking clearly — and coercing you becomes liberating you. Berlin had watched that argument used by states that called their prisons schools.

He was not calling positive liberty worthless: the two are separate goods that genuinely conflict, which makes him a pluralist rather than a libertarian.

The counter-punch is fair. Charles Taylor argued in 1979 that pure negative liberty cannot tell a traffic light from a censorship law, since both are interferences.

recall.question: What is Berlin's specific worry about positive liberty?

options.text: That it requires redistribution
options.why: Berlin's argument is not about economics.

options.text: That self-mastery can be hijacked
options.why: someone else defines your "real" self and then coerces you in its name.

options.text: That it is incoherent
options.why: Berlin treats it as a genuine value, in real conflict with negative liberty.

phil.political.nozick.liberty-upsets-pat.title: Liberty upsets patterns
phil.political.nozick.liberty-upsets-pat.hook: Start from whatever distribution you think is perfectly just. Nozick shows it survives about one basketball season.
phil.political.nozick.liberty-upsets-pat.author: author-humanities-1
phil.political.nozick.liberty-upsets-pat.body:
Robert Nozick, writing against Rawls in *Anarchy, State, and Utopia* (1974), offers a deal. Pick any distribution of wealth you consider perfectly just. Strict equality, the difference principle, anything — call it D1, and stipulate it is ideal.

Now: a million people each drop an extra 25 cents in a box to watch Wilt Chamberlain play basketball. Nobody is tricked or coerced, and every holding was just to begin with. Chamberlain ends the season with an extra \$250,000, and the distribution is now D2, unequal and by your own standard unjust.

Which transaction was wrong? Nozick's conclusion: no **patterned** principle — one demanding the distribution always match a formula — survives without forbidding voluntary transfers or continuously undoing them. Justice is therefore historical: a holding is just if acquired and transferred justly, whatever shape results.

G. A. Cohen's reply is that the argument assumes its baseline. The fans spend money held under one particular property regime, and whether Chamberlain may charge at all is exactly what was in dispute.

recall.question: What is Nozick's Wilt Chamberlain argument meant to show?

options.text: That equality makes people worse off
options.why: the argument is about justice, not efficiency or incentives.

options.text: That any pattern-based principle collides with voluntary transfers
options.why: keeping the pattern means constantly blocking or reversing free exchanges.

options.text: That the rich deserve their wealth by talent
options.why: Nozick's entitlement theory turns on how holdings arose, not on desert.

phil.political.rawls.design-a-society-yo.title: Choose the rules before you know who you will be
phil.political.rawls.design-a-society-yo.hook: Design the society first, then find out who you are in it. Rawls turns fairness into a decision problem under uncertainty.
phil.political.rawls.design-a-society-yo.author: author-humanities-1
phil.political.rawls.design-a-society-yo.body:
Rawls's move in *A Theory of Justice* (1971) is a trick for removing bias without asking anyone to be nice. You are choosing the basic institutions of a society — property, taxes, liberties, courts — from behind a **veil of ignorance**. You do not know your class, race, sex, talents, health, or even which conception of the good life you will end up holding. You know general facts about economics and psychology, and nothing about your own ticket.

Self-interest now does the work of impartiality. Endorsing a rule that crushes the bottom means endorsing it for a position you might occupy.

Rawls argues the parties pick two principles, in strict order. First, the most extensive basic liberties compatible with the same for everyone — absolutely first, so no amount of wealth buys a cut in anyone's basic freedoms. Second, inequalities are allowed only if they attach to positions open to all under fair equality of opportunity, and only if they benefit the least advantaged most. That is the **difference principle**: inequality is not forbidden, it is required to pay rent.

The step from the veil to those principles is the contested one.
phil.political.rawls.design-a-society-yo.rigor:
Behind the veil, the choice is a decision under uncertainty over social positions. Rawls argues for **maximin**: rank institutions by the welfare of their worst-off position and take the best of those,
$$\max_{\text{institutions } I} \; \min_{\text{positions } i} \; u_i(I),$$
on the grounds that the situation is one of genuine ignorance rather than known risk, that the stakes at the bottom are catastrophic, and that gains above a decent minimum matter little.

John Harsanyi's 1975 objection is direct. If you are ignorant of your position, treat the positions as equiprobable — his "equiprobability" postulate — and expected-utility reasoning then gives
$$\max_{I} \; \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} u_i(I),$$
which is average utilitarianism, not maximin. Maximin, he argued, is an irrational decision rule outside of games against a malevolent opponent: it would forbid you from ever crossing a street.

Rawls's defence is that the veil is not a lottery. There is no well-defined probability over being born as someone, the choice is made once and binds a whole life, and the parties must be able to honestly commit to whatever they choose — a "strains of commitment" condition that rules out gambles you could not live with. Which of the two arguments you accept determines whether the original position delivers Rawls's conclusions or Harsanyi's.

recall.question: What does the difference principle actually permit?

options.text: Only strictly equal distributions
options.why: Rawls explicitly allows inequality, on a condition.

options.text: Inequalities that make the worst-off position better than it would be under any alternative
options.why: inequality has to earn its keep from the bottom up.

options.text: Whatever maximises total welfare
options.why: that is utilitarianism, and it is the position Rawls is arguing against.

sources.title: Can the Maximin Principle Serve as a Basis for Morality? A Critique of John Rawls's Theory
sources.author: John C. Harsanyi

phil.political.rawls.the-first-virtue.title: Justice is the first virtue of social institutions
phil.political.rawls.the-first-virtue.hook: The opening line of the most important work of political philosophy of the twentieth century.
phil.political.rawls.the-first-virtue.author: author-humanities-1
phil.political.rawls.the-first-virtue.body:
> "Justice is the first virtue of social institutions, as truth is of systems of thought."

John Rawls, opening *A Theory of Justice* (1971), page 3.

The analogy is the argument in miniature. An elegant theory that is false gets thrown out, however elegant. Rawls says an efficient, prosperous, well-loved institution that is unjust should go the same way — and the rest of the book is an attempt to say what "unjust" means precisely enough to hold that line.

phil.science.demarcation-popper.popper-w.title: Remember falsifiability? Here is a field that stopped doing it
phil.science.demarcation-popper.popper-w.hook: Remember falsifiability? The replication crisis is what a field looks like when it keeps Popper's words and drops his procedure.
phil.science.demarcation-popper.popper-w.author: author-humanities-1
phil.science.demarcation-popper.popper-w.body:
Popper's demand was that a theory forbid something, and that you go looking for the thing it forbids. Statistical significance testing was supposed to be exactly that, industrialised: fix a prediction, run the experiment, let a small p-value count as a failed attempt to refute.

Then note what a career rewards. Choose the outcome measure after seeing the data. Drop the conditions that failed. Add participants until the test crosses the line. Write the introduction so the result you found is the one you predicted — Norbert Kerr named that HARKing in 1998. Each keeps the vocabulary of refutation while removing its possibility: the hypothesis is fitted to the data, not exposed to it.

The measurement arrived in 2015. The Open Science Collaboration ran 100 replications of psychology studies: 97% of the originals reported significant effects, and 36% of the replications did. John Ioannidis had predicted the shape of this in 2005 from the arithmetic of low power, small effects and many analytic choices.

The cure is old-fashioned. Preregistration is falsifiability as paperwork: say in advance what would count as failure, so the world can still say no.

recall.question: In what sense is preregistration a Popperian device?

options.text: It guarantees the result will replicate
options.why: it does not; it only stops the prediction from being rewritten after the fact.

options.text: It fixes the prediction and the analysis before the data exist
options.why: which is what makes a genuine refutation possible.

options.text: It raises statistical power
options.why: power is a separate fix, and a preregistered study can still be underpowered.

sources.title: Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science
sources.author: Open Science Collaboration

sources.title: Why Most Published Research Findings Are False
sources.author: John P. A. Ioannidis

phil.science.demarcation-popper.what-wou.title: What would have to happen for you to give this up?
phil.science.demarcation-popper.what-wou.hook: Popper's question is one line long and it still sorts the room: what observation would make you abandon this?
phil.science.demarcation-popper.what-wou.author: author-humanities-1
phil.science.demarcation-popper.what-wou.body:
Vienna, 1919. Karl Popper, then a young man, was surrounded by theories that explained everything: Marxist history, Adler's psychology. A man pushes a child into a river; a man dies saving one. The theory accounts for both, easily, every time. That explanatory power impressed everyone else and worried him.

Then Eddington's eclipse expedition tested Einstein. Light bends by the predicted amount, or general relativity is finished. Einstein had staked it on something that could go wrong.

That is the criterion. A scientific theory forbids things, and the more it forbids the more it says. Confirmations are cheap: look and you will find them.

The criterion does not survive practice, and Popper knew it. You never test a hypothesis alone: it comes bundled with instruments and auxiliary assumptions, so a failure never says which part to blame. The wobble in Uranus's orbit could have refuted Newton. Astronomers blamed an unseen planet and found Neptune. The same move applied to Mercury's perihelion, and that planet was never there. Imre Lakatos rebuilt the idea around research programmes, judged over time by whether they keep predicting new things.

recall.question: What does the Duhem-Quine problem do to naive falsificationism?

options.text: It shows theories can never be confirmed
options.why: confirmation was never Popper's criterion in the first place.

options.text: A failed prediction refutes the whole bundle of hypothesis plus auxiliaries
options.why: so it never tells you which element to reject.

options.text: It shows scientists are irrational when they keep a refuted theory
options.why: Lakatos argues the opposite: protecting a programme can be rational while it still predicts.

phil.science.kuhn-paradigms.the-word-tha.title: The word that got away from the man who coined it
phil.science.kuhn-paradigms.the-word-tha.hook: Kuhn wrote a book about how key terms shift meaning across revolutions. A critic counted twenty-one meanings of his own key term inside it.
phil.science.kuhn-paradigms.the-word-tha.author: author-humanities-1
phil.science.kuhn-paradigms.the-word-tha.body:
Thomas Kuhn's *The Structure of Scientific Revolutions* came out in 1962, oddly enough as a monograph in a logical-positivist encyclopedia series. Its picture: science is not a steady accumulation. Most of the time researchers do **normal science**, solving puzzles inside a shared framework and treating failures as their own fault rather than the framework's. Anomalies pile up, a crisis arrives, and a revolution installs a new framework whose practitioners ask different questions and no longer fully understand the old answers. That last part is **incommensurability**, and it is what made the book famous and suspect at once.

Then Margaret Masterman, in a 1970 paper, went through the text and counted at least twenty-one distinct senses of "paradigm" — from a whole worldview down to a single worked exemplar in a textbook. Kuhn accepted the hit and, in the 1970 postscript, split the word in two: the **disciplinary matrix** a community shares, and the **exemplars**, the concrete solved problems students learn by imitating.

The irony is perfect and instructive. A book arguing that terms quietly change meaning when frameworks shift had a term that changed meaning inside a single volume.

recall.question: What does Kuhn mean by "normal science"?

options.text: Science done without major discoveries
options.why: plenty of discovery happens in normal science; what is fixed is the framework.

options.text: Puzzle-solving within an accepted framework
options.why: where a failure counts against the researcher rather than against the paradigm.

options.text: The period before a field has any paradigm
options.why: Kuhn calls that the pre-paradigm phase, which is different.

phil.science.models-idealization.all-mod.title: All models are wrong, but some are useful
phil.science.models-idealization.all-mod.hook: The most quoted sentence in statistics. The clause that does the work is the second one.
phil.science.models-idealization.all-mod.author: author-humanities-1

reviewed.notes: Hook claimed people usually drop the second clause, which is not true - the line is quoted whole. Rewritten to point at which clause does the work.

phil.science.models-idealization.all-mod.body:
> "Essentially, all models are wrong, but some are useful."

George Box and Norman Draper, *Empirical Model-Building and Response Surfaces* (Wiley, 1987), page 424. The thought runs through Box's 1976 paper in the *Journal of the American Statistical Association* too, where he warns against chasing correctness by adding elaboration.

The second clause is the working half. It replaces "is this model true?", which always answers no, with "is it wrong in a way that matters for what I am about to do with it?"

sources.title: Empirical Model-Building and Response Surfaces
sources.author: George E. P. Box and Norman R. Draper
